claims.text: Transition-metal catalyst activity is governed by the surface oxidation state and local coordination environment.
Transition-metal catalyst selectivity is governed by the surface oxidation state and local coordination environment.
Surface oxidation state and local coordination modulate active-site electronic structure, especially d-orbital occupancy.
Changes in active-site electronic structure control the adsorption strength of reaction intermediates.
Annealing in an oxidizing atmosphere induces surface oxidation and modifies surface coordination.
Annealing in a reducing atmosphere maintains a predominantly metallic surface state.
Oxidizing treatment creates a controlled surface oxide layer.
The surface oxide layer modifies d-orbital occupancy.
Modified d-orbital occupancy changes the binding energies of reaction intermediates.
An optimal degree of surface modification improves the adsorption-desorption balance.
An improved adsorption-desorption balance increases catalytic turnover and selectivity.
A predominantly metallic surface produces reaction kinetics different from those of an oxidized surface.
Mildly oxidized catalysts will have higher turnover frequency than reducing-annealed catalysts.
Mildly oxidized catalysts will have greater product selectivity than reducing-annealed catalysts.
The predicted improvement results from favorable modification of active-site electronic properties.
The hypothesis applies to transition-metal nanoparticles under ambient reaction conditions only within an oxidation-state window that avoids inactive over-oxidized phases.
XPS can be used to characterize surface oxidation state and aspects of the coordination environment.
TEM can be used to assess particle morphology and dispersion.
Failure of oxidizing treatment to produce a statistically significant activity and selectivity improvement would falsify the hypothesis.
Absence of a correlation between oxidation state or coordination environment and catalytic performance would falsify the hypothesis.
